examples.problem:
Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln{2x}}{x}$ (plotted below) is strictly increasing.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/2ccb7c95d06c78a1730f9ca46aad9b6f1370050c745f2c1fc9208275670c3649.png)
examples.worked_solution:
To find where $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, we need to solve the inequality $f'(x) > 0.$

Differentiating $f(x)$ using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x})\cdot x-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot 1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2x}{{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

 

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\dfrac{1-\ln{2x}}{x^2} > 0.
$$

The denominator is  always positive, so this reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2x>0\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2x<1.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving $\ln{2x} = 1$ gives the critical point

$$
2x = e\quad \Longrightarrow\quad x = \dfrac{1}{2}e.
$$

From the graph, we see that this critical point is a maximum. We also see that the slope of the tangent lines is positive to the left of the critical point and negative to the right of the critical point. 

We summarize this information in the following table:

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}x & (0,\frac{1}{2}e) & \frac{1}{2}e & (\frac{1}{2}e,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & -\end{aligned}\right|
$$

Finally, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the interval $\left(0,\frac 1 2 e\right),$ which can also be written as $0 < x < \dfrac 1 2 e.$

feedback.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=5-7x-4{x}^{2}$ is strictly decreasing.
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-7-8x \\  & =-8(x+\frac{7}{8}),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
-8(x+\frac{7}{8})<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8(x+\frac{7}{8}) & <0 \\ 0 & <8(x+\frac{7}{8}) \\ 0 & <x+\frac{7}{8} \\ -\frac{7}{8} & <x.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $x\in (-\frac{7}{8},\infty ).$
